title: From Relief to Resilience: How Bharat transformed its disaster management
excerpt: India’s disaster management framework has undergone a significant transformation since 2014, with a growing emphasis on preparedness, prevention, risk reduction and resilience rather than relying primarily on relief and rehabilitation after disasters. Over the past decade, policy reforms, technological advancements, disaster-resilient infrastructure, community participation and increased financial allocations have contributed to strengthening the country’s ability to respond to natural calamities. The changing approach was highlighted on October 28, 2026, when Cyclone Arnab struck the Andhra Pradesh-Yanam coast. Timely weather forecasting, advance evacuation measures, coordinated government action and the rapid deployment of National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) and State Disaster Response Force (SDRF) teams helped minimise casualties and damage. The response reflected the importance of early-warning mechanisms, institutional coordination and preparedness in managing severe weather events. A major component of this transformation has been the development of a comprehensive institutional framework. The National Disaster Management Plan (NDMP), introduced in 2016 and aligned with the United Nations Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction 2015-2030, established a structured approach to understanding disaster risks, strengthening governance, investing in risk reduction and improving preparedness. The Prime Minister’s Ten-Point Agenda for Disaster Risk Reduction, presented in November 2016, further emphasised integrating disaster management into development planning and strengthening institutional capabilities. Community participation has also emerged as an important part of India’s disaster preparedness strategy. Through the Aapda Mitra scheme, the initial pilot programme covering 5,186 volunteers across 30 districts expanded towards a target of one lakh trained, certified and insured community volunteers across 350 multi-hazard-prone districts. The Yuva Aapda Mitra initiative further involved the National Cadet Corps (NCC), National Service Scheme (NSS) and Bharat Scouts and Guides in disaster preparedness and response activities. Alongside institutional and community-level reforms, India strengthened disaster-resilient infrastructure across coastal, riverine and Himalayan regions. Multi-purpose cyclone shelters, evacuation roads, bridges, underground electricity cables, saline embankments, river protection measures, slope stabilisation structures and rockfall barriers were developed to reduce the vulnerability of communities and essential infrastructure in disaster-prone areas. Technological advancements also expanded the country’s early-warning capabilities. Doppler weather radars, tsunami monitoring systems, storm-surge modelling, satellite-based drought assessment, heatwave alerts and the Damini lightning-warning application strengthened the mechanisms for identifying and communicating potential threats. Mission Mausam, approved in September 2024 with an allocation of Rs.2,000 crore, further aims to modernise weather and climate forecasting through artificial intelligence, high-performance computing and expanded radar networks. Financial assistance and emergency response mechanisms also received greater attention. During the 2021-2026 award period, Rs.1,60,153 crore was allocated to State Disaster Risk Management Funds, while Rs.54,770 crore was allocated to the National Disaster Response Fund (NDRF) and Rs.13,693 crore to the National Disaster Mitigation Fund (NDMF). Meanwhile, the average deployment time of Inter-Ministerial Central Teams (IMCTs) declined from 96 days to eight days by 2025, accelerating central assessment following disasters. From the introduction of institutional reforms and community-based response programmes to the expansion of early-warning technology, resilient infrastructure and financial support, these developments represent important milestones in India’s disaster management journey. The detailed From Relief to Resilience: How India Strengthened Disaster Preparedness Since 2014, is given below. India’s Progress in Disaster Risk Reduction and Resilience Building India’s disaster governance system has undergone significant improvements since 2014, with a shift in focus from providing relief after disasters to strengthening preparedness, early-warning systems, risk reduction and faster emergency response. The approach has increasingly focused on minimising the loss of human lives and property through improved planning, coordination and institutional mechanisms. Before 2014, India’s disaster management system remained fragmented and largely reactive. Despite the enactment of the Disaster Management Act, 2005, disaster management authorities lacked proper coordination, adequate staffing and a unified operational plan. These shortcomings resulted in delayed responses and uncoordinated relief operations during major disasters. A significant change came in May 2016, when India introduced its first comprehensive National Disaster Management Plan (NDMP). The plan was subsequently updated in November 2019 to incorporate climate change considerations, local disaster risks and improved disaster management strategies. The NDMP aligned India’s disaster management strategy with the four priorities of the United Nations Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction 2015-2030. These priorities included understanding disaster risks, improving disaster management systems, investing in disaster risk reduction and strengthening preparedness for effective response. The plan also adopted the principle of Build Back Better during recovery, rehabilitation and reconstruction. The implementation of this international commitment was further driven by the Prime Minister’s Ten-Point Agenda for Disaster Risk Reduction, articulated at the Asian Ministerial Conference on Disaster Risk Reduction held in New Delhi in November 2016. The agenda called for the integration of disaster risk management into the work of all development sectors. It also emphasised protecting poor households and small and medium-sized businesses, increasing women’s leadership in disaster management, and investing in multi-hazard mapping, technology and stronger institutional mechanisms. Community-Level Preparedness, Training and Public Participation The Central Government, through the National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA), launched the Aapda Mitra scheme to train local residents to act as first responders during disasters. Initially implemented as a pilot programme between 2016 and 2018, the scheme covered 5,186 volunteers across 30 flood-prone districts in 25 states. The scheme was subsequently expanded nationwide, with a target of training, certifying and equipping 1,00,000 community volunteers across 350 multi-hazard-prone districts in all states and Union Territories. Under the programme, volunteers receive a five-day training course conducted by master trainers from the State Disaster Response Force (SDRF) and National Disaster Response Force (NDRF). The training covers first aid, cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR), basic search and rescue, navigation through collapsed structures, flood rescue operations and the evacuation of vulnerable people. Trained volunteers are provided with an Emergency Responder Kit containing protective gear, safety helmets, life jackets, LED torches, first-aid equipment, multi-tool knives and emergency whistles. Each enrolled volunteer is also provided with three years of life and disability insurance coverage. Aapda Mitra volunteers have assisted local authorities during several disasters, including Cyclone Fani in Odisha, the Kerala floods and the Wayanad landslide. title: NIELIT to organise 3rd international conference on cyber security, digital forensics and intelligence in New Delhi tomorrow
excerpt: New Delhi, Nov 15: The National Institute of Electronics & Information Technology (NIELIT), under the Ministry of Electronics & Information Technology (MeitY), Government of India, is organising the 3rd National Conference on Cyber Security, Digital Forensics & Intelligence (NCCDFI 2026) on November 16-17, 2026, at the Dr. Ambedkar International Centre, 15 Janpath, New Delhi, centered around the theme “Cyber Secure Bharat: Fortifying India’s Digital Future. The conference assumes noteworthy significance in the present digital era, wherein the increasing dependence on digital technologies, the emergence of sophisticated cyber threats and the evolving nature of cybercrime have made cyber security and digital investigation critical areas of national importance. The journey of NCCDFI began in 2024 with its inaugural edition in Kohima, Nagaland, held from 25–26 July 2024 at the Capital Convention Centre, Organised by NIELIT Kohima in collaboration with the Nagaland Police and the Department of Information Technology & Communication, Government of Nagaland. Building on the foundation laid in Kohima, the second edition of NCCDFI was held in 2025 at Gauhati University, Guwahati, Assam. Drawing on the success of its preceding editions, the conference expanded its reach from a regional initiative into a broader national platform. The third edition aims to further strengthen this platform through wider participation, technology demonstrations, knowledge exchange and stronger collaboration among key stakeholders. NCCDFI 2026 will provide a knowledge-sharing platform for stakeholders from government, law enforcement, defence, judiciary, technology providers, industry, academia and the cybersecurity ecosystem to deliberate on emerging cyber threats and evolving challenges in digital investigations and cyber resilience. The conference will focus on strengthening coordination among agencies, enhancing capacity in cybersecurity and digital forensics, facilitating policy dialogue and exploring the application of emerging technologies such as Artificial Intelligence, Blockchain Security and Cyber Intelligence. NCCDFI 2026 is supported by a strong group of industry partners, bringing together leading organisations in digital forensics, cybersecurity and investigative technologies. The knowledge partners includes Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre (I4C), CERT-In, Delhi Police, CyberPeace, Standardisation Testing and Quality Certification (STQC), Military College of Telecommunication Engineering (MCTE), Mhow, Maharashtra Cyber, Manipur Police, Telangana Cyber Security Bureau (TGCSB), Hyderabad, Software Technology Parks of India (STPI) and Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship (MSDE). The industry partners includes STELLAR, Power Forensics & Digital Intelligence, Magnet Forensics, MSAB, Cyint Technologies, 3rd Eye Techno Solutions, Advanced Digital Forensic Solutions, Inc., Oxygen Forensics and VERTEXON LABS. Their participation will contribute industry expertise, technology demonstrations and practical insights, strengthening the conference’s focus on advancing capabilities in cybersecurity, digital forensics and digital investigations. The conference will focus on 10 key tracks covering the evolving cybersecurity landscape: Cybersecurity, Digital Forensics, AI Security, Critical Infrastructure, Threat Intelligence, Blockchain & Crypto, Drone & IoT Forensics, Digital Evidence, Cyber Law, and Cloud Security. These tracks will bring together experts and practitioners to explore emerging threats, technological advancements, investigative techniques, regulatory developments and strategies for building a secure and resilient digital ecosystem. The two-day conference will feature an inaugural session, technical and business sessions, panel discussions, an industry exhibition and Cyber Kushti 2026 – Cybersecurity & AI Hackathon. The technical sessions will cover key areas including national cybersecurity and critical infrastructure, incident response, AI-enabled cyber threats, automated digital investigations, cyber threat intelligence, financial cybercrime, advanced device and multimedia forensics, law-enforcement readiness, international cooperation, digital evidence, quantum computing, autonomous systems, frontier technologies, capacity building and the national cyber ecosystem. The exhibition during the conference will showcase technologies and solutions in digital forensics, cybersecurity, drone technology, surveillance systems and AI-driven security, with opportunities for technical interactions and business-to-business engagements. A key highlight of NCCDFI 2026, “Cyber Kushti 2026- Cybersecurity & AI Hackathon”, will be organised alongside the technical sessions. The three-level competition is structured around the themes of Review, Attack and Defend, reflecting critical aspects of modern cybersecurity operations. The hackathon has received an overwhelming response, with 1,031 teams comprising 3,093 participants registering for the competition. Of these, 923 teams (2,769 participants) have been shortlisted for Level 1, while 50 teams have qualified for Level 2 and 10 teams for Level 3. NCCDFI 2026 will also feature the signing of MoUs between NIELIT and industry partners, aimed at strengthening institutional partnership, knowledge exchange, joint initiatives, research and development, and capacity building in the fields of cyber security, digital forensics & intelligence, etc. These collaborations are envisaged to establish a framework for long-term cooperation and facilitate industry-academia engagement and promote future collaborative initiatives in these critical domains. Through NCCDFI 2026, NIELIT along with its supporting organisations and institutional partners, seeks to contribute towards strengthening professional competencies, fostering institutional collaboration and supporting the development of a secure, resilient and trusted digital ecosystem in the country.

title: From Relief to Resilience: How Bharat transformed its disaster management
excerpt: India’s disaster management framework has undergone a significant transformation since 2014, with a growing emphasis on preparedness, prevention, risk reduction and resilience rather than relying primarily on relief and rehabilitation after disasters. Over the past decade, policy reforms, technological advancements, disaster-resilient infrastructure, community participation and increased financial allocations have contributed to strengthening the country’s ability to respond to natural calamities. The changing approach was highlighted on October 28, 2026, when Cyclone Arnab struck the Andhra Pradesh-Yanam coast. Timely weather forecasting, advance evacuation measures, coordinated government action and the rapid deployment of National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) and State Disaster Response Force (SDRF) teams helped minimise casualties and damage. The response reflected the importance of early-warning mechanisms, institutional coordination and preparedness in managing severe weather events. A major component of this transformation has been the development of a comprehensive institutional framework. The National Disaster Management Plan (NDMP), introduced in 2016 and aligned with the United Nations Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction 2015-2030, established a structured approach to understanding disaster risks, strengthening governance, investing in risk reduction and improving preparedness. The Prime Minister’s Ten-Point Agenda for Disaster Risk Reduction, presented in November 2016, further emphasised integrating disaster management into development planning and strengthening institutional capabilities. Community participation has also emerged as an important part of India’s disaster preparedness strategy. Through the Aapda Mitra scheme, the initial pilot programme covering 5,186 volunteers across 30 districts expanded towards a target of one lakh trained, certified and insured community volunteers across 350 multi-hazard-prone districts. The Yuva Aapda Mitra initiative further involved the National Cadet Corps (NCC), National Service Scheme (NSS) and Bharat Scouts and Guides in disaster preparedness and response activities. Alongside institutional and community-level reforms, India strengthened disaster-resilient infrastructure across coastal, riverine and Himalayan regions. Multi-purpose cyclone shelters, evacuation roads, bridges, underground electricity cables, saline embankments, river protection measures, slope stabilisation structures and rockfall barriers were developed to reduce the vulnerability of communities and essential infrastructure in disaster-prone areas. Technological advancements also expanded the country’s early-warning capabilities. Doppler weather radars, tsunami monitoring systems, storm-surge modelling, satellite-based drought assessment, heatwave alerts and the Damini lightning-warning application strengthened the mechanisms for identifying and communicating potential threats. Mission Mausam, approved in September 2024 with an allocation of Rs.2,000 crore, further aims to modernise weather and climate forecasting through artificial intelligence, high-performance computing and expanded radar networks. Financial assistance and emergency response mechanisms also received greater attention. During the 2021-2026 award period, Rs.1,60,153 crore was allocated to State Disaster Risk Management Funds, while Rs.54,770 crore was allocated to the National Disaster Response Fund (NDRF) and Rs.13,693 crore to the National Disaster Mitigation Fund (NDMF). Meanwhile, the average deployment time of Inter-Ministerial Central Teams (IMCTs) declined from 96 days to eight days by 2025, accelerating central assessment following disasters. From the introduction of institutional reforms and community-based response programmes to the expansion of early-warning technology, resilient infrastructure and financial support, these developments represent important milestones in India’s disaster management journey. title: NIELIT to organise 3rd international conference on cyber security, digital forensics and intelligence in New Delhi tomorrow
excerpt: New Delhi, Nov 15: The National Institute of Electronics & Information Technology (NIELIT), under the Ministry of Electronics & Information Technology (MeitY), Government of India, is organising the 3rd National Conference on Cyber Security, Digital Forensics & Intelligence (NCCDFI 2026) on November 16-17, 2026, at the Dr. Ambedkar International Centre, 15 Janpath, New Delhi, centered around the theme “Cyber Secure Bharat: Fortifying India’s Digital Future. The conference assumes noteworthy significance in the present digital era, wherein the increasing dependence on digital technologies, the emergence of sophisticated cyber threats and the evolving nature of cybercrime have made cyber security and digital investigation critical areas of national importance. The journey of NCCDFI began in 2024 with its inaugural edition in Kohima, Nagaland, held from 25–26 July 2024 at the Capital Convention Centre, Organised by NIELIT Kohima in collaboration with the Nagaland Police and the Department of Information Technology & Communication, Government of Nagaland. Building on the foundation laid in Kohima, the second edition of NCCDFI was held in 2025 at Gauhati University, Guwahati, Assam. Drawing on the success of its preceding editions, the conference expanded its reach from a regional initiative into a broader national platform. The third edition aims to further strengthen this platform through wider participation, technology demonstrations, knowledge exchange and stronger collaboration among key stakeholders. NCCDFI 2026 will provide a knowledge-sharing platform for stakeholders from government, law enforcement, defence, judiciary, technology providers, industry, academia and the cybersecurity ecosystem to deliberate on emerging cyber threats and evolving challenges in digital investigations and cyber resilience. The conference will focus on strengthening coordination among agencies, enhancing capacity in cybersecurity and digital forensics, facilitating policy dialogue and exploring the application of emerging technologies such as Artificial Intelligence, Blockchain Security and Cyber Intelligence. NCCDFI 2026 is supported by a strong group of industry partners, bringing together leading organisations in digital forensics, cybersecurity and investigative technologies. The knowledge partners includes Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre (I4C), CERT-In, Delhi Police, CyberPeace, Standardisation Testing and Quality Certification (STQC), Military College of Telecommunication Engineering (MCTE), Mhow, Maharashtra Cyber, Manipur Police, Telangana Cyber Security Bureau (TGCSB), Hyderabad, Software Technology Parks of India (STPI) and Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship (MSDE). The industry partners includes STELLAR, Power Forensics & Digital Intelligence, Magnet Forensics, MSAB, Cyint Technologies, 3rd Eye Techno Solutions, Advanced Digital Forensic Solutions, Inc., Oxygen Forensics and VERTEXON LABS. Their participation will contribute industry expertise, technology demonstrations and practical insights, strengthening the conference’s focus on advancing capabilities in cybersecurity, digital forensics and digital investigations. The conference will focus on 10 key tracks covering the evolving cybersecurity landscape: Cybersecurity, Digital Forensics, AI Security, Critical Infrastructure, Threat Intelligence, Blockchain & Crypto, Drone & IoT Forensics, Digital Evidence, Cyber Law, and Cloud Security. These tracks will bring together experts and practitioners to explore emerging threats, technological advancements, investigative techniques, regulatory developments and strategies for building a secure and resilient digital ecosystem. The two-day conference will feature an inaugural session, technical and business sessions, panel discussions, an industry exhibition and Cyber Kushti 2026 – Cybersecurity & AI Hackathon. The technical sessions will cover key areas including national cybersecurity and critical infrastructure, incident response, AI-enabled cyber threats, automated digital investigations, cyber threat intelligence, financial cybercrime, advanced device and multimedia forensics, law-enforcement readiness, international cooperation, digital evidence, quantum computing, autonomous systems, frontier technologies, capacity building and the national cyber ecosystem. The exhibition during the conference will showcase technologies and solutions in digital forensics, cybersecurity, drone technology, surveillance systems and AI-driven security, with opportunities for technical interactions and business-to-business engagements. A key highlight of NCCDFI 2026, “Cyber Kushti 2026- Cybersecurity & AI Hackathon”, will be organised alongside the technical sessions. The three-level competition is structured around the themes of Review, Attack and Defend, reflecting critical aspects of modern cybersecurity operations. The hackathon has received an overwhelming response, with 1,031 teams comprising 3,093 participants registering for the competition. Of these, 923 teams (2,769 participants) have been shortlisted for Level 1, while 50 teams have qualified for Level 2 and 10 teams for Level 3. NCCDFI 2026 will also feature the signing of MoUs between NIELIT and industry partners, aimed at strengthening institutional partnership, knowledge exchange, joint initiatives, research and development, and capacity building in the fields of cyber security, digital forensics & intelligence, etc. These collaborations are envisaged to establish a framework for long-term cooperation and facilitate industry-academia engagement and promote future collaborative initiatives in these critical domains. Through NCCDFI 2026, NIELIT along with its supporting organisations and institutional partners, seeks to contribute towards strengthening professional competencies, fostering institutional collaboration and supporting the development of a secure, resilient and trusted digital ecosystem in the country.

title: Truffello Is the Carter Road Pasta Bar With A Speakeasy Spirit
excerpt: Saturdays are usually for me to bed-rot: catching up on a week’s sleep (even if well slept), cooking something easy and going back to bed with a movie or two. Last Saturday, I had to ditch the routine and head to Truffello, a pasta bar that has opened on Carter Road, Bandra. A newly opened space wasn’t the novelty I was looking for. I wanted to know why my co-workers kept pushing me to check it out. I walked in with high expectations and was hit with the smell of truffle. It’s a setting you wouldn’t anticipate from the street. The People Behind It Truffello was conceived by Kanchan, who comes from a fashion background, with architecture and interiors led by her husband Dhivesh of Space Design. The restaurant pairs that atmosphere with fresh pasta, hand-stretched pizza and a thoughtfully curated coffee menu. Kanchan brings the vision and her fashion eye, while Dhivesh shaped the space with Space Design. Together they’ve built an intimate Italian table with the intrigue of a speakeasy, in a neighbourhood that rarely slows down. What I Ate The menu is decent and covers antipasti, pasta, risotto, gnocchi and more. I can’t have it all alone, so I brought my roommate along. For appetizers, we called for the Mushroom Croquette, Chicken Parmesan Meatballs and Stuffed Chicken Wings. As we waited, I realised the smell of truffles never left. They are clearly generous with it. Personally, I’m not a fan, so do take what I say with a pinch of salt. I’d enjoy the Mushroom Croquette without the truffle aioli, but with it, the aioli overpowers the dish completely. That did force me to sip on my drink, and I’m not complaining. The Rosso Riviera is the best drink to pair with the meal because the lemon in it cuts through the richness. The Chicken Parmesan Meatballs were slightly underseasoned, but the marinara sauce balances them well. I could happily have just the marinara with the parmesan: perfectly tangy, with a subtle heat. The Stuffed Chicken Wings were my favourite. They were crispy and tossed in just the right amount of house hot sauce. The stuffing is similar to the meatballs, but more herby, and I genuinely enjoyed finishing the plate. Before the mains came, I sipped on the Amalfi Bloom to clear my tastebuds. It’s a perfect sip when the Mumbai heat is out to get you. For the mains, we ordered Truffello’s Spaghetti and the Rainbow Ravioli. The spaghetti has a slight bite, and the sauce is perfect if you love truffle. If you’re like me, a squeeze of lemon will balance everything out. It’s a vegetarian dish on the menu, but you can add chicken. I’m happy I did, because the chicken was perfectly cooked and gives the pepper in the sauce something to latch on to. It’s a heavy meal, and the earthiness of the mushroom stock will have you going for seconds. I consciously took a step back because I still had one main and dessert to go. The Rainbow Ravioli was another favourite, again because of the marinara sauce. It leans cheesier, with the stracciatella and pecorino in the dish. There are also good seafood options. The Pizza Ai Frutti Di Mare, a mixed seafood pizza, and the Risotto Alla Milanese, with saffron-infused stock and pan-seared prawns, were staff picks. I didn’t order them because of my allergies, and yes, I wished things were different so I could feel exactly what the neighbouring table felt when they had these. For dessert, the Nocciola is the right way to end the meal: silky chocolate mousse and hazelnut gelato, sweet, nutty and as rich as everything before it. If you like it classic, go for the Tiramisu. The Space The space is small, with 20 seats and the open kitchen as its anchor. It was full within 20 minutes of my arrival. The warm lighting and soft music set the tone, as if you were at the house of a friend who loves everything Italy. ELLE Gourmet’s Verdict Truffello works for dates and for days when you feel indulgent. I enjoyed the meal, and it’s a place I’ll keep in mind if one of my friends craves truffles. Where: Shop No. 1 and 1A, Gaganiri Premises Co-op. Hsg, Soc. Ltd, Sangeet Samrat Naushad Ali Rd, Union Park, Khar West, Mumbai, Maharashtra 400052 Timings: 12–4 pm & 6 pm–12 am Cost for two: INR 2,800 - INR 3,800
